To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
rubrospinal axons degenerate in the cervical cord after partial or complete stereoxatic lesions of the red nucleus.
rubrospinal fibers terminate on dendritic spines and shafts in the LBR.

1) rubrospinal axon terminals in the LBR are not specific for dendritic profiles of a certain size; 2) the LBR is a region of high density of rubrospinals; and 3) the rubrospinals are not the only afferent system that synapses on the LBR.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fine structure of the rubrosphinal terminals in the spinal cord of the cat.
the fine structure of the rubral projections to the cervical cord of cats.
the ultrastructural analysis of the degenerating rubrospinal axon terminals in the LBR of the cat's cervical cord.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the rubrospinals are axosomatic, axodendritic, and axosomatic axodendritic in their termination in the spinal cord.
rubrospinal axons do not terminate on the anterior horn motor cells in the spinal grey matter but on the inter-neurons, mostly in LBR.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the rubrospinothalamic pathway is a direct route for the transmission of information from the red nucleus to the motor cortex, and the rubrospineuronal pathway is the indirect route via the spinal cord.

the fine structure of rubrospinothalamic terminals is not different from the rubrospino-cervical terminals in their early stages of degeneration and that the rubrospiral fibers do not terminate on the large motor neurons but on the LBR neurons in the lateral portion in Rexed's laminae V-VII.
rubrospinal axons in the cat terminate in the LBR of Rexed's V-VII laminae and the terminals have a distinctive ultrastructure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the rubrospiral tract does not directly innervate motor neurons in the cervical cord, and instead it targets interneurons in Rexed's laminae of V-VII.
the rubrospiral tract is not the main pathway for the control of the motor neurons.
the rubrospinals are not the primary pathway for motor control, but instead are more involved in sensory processing.
